questions.explain: join is a STRING method: separator.join(list). '-'.join([...]) glues the pieces with '-' between them. Coming from JS this feels backwards (arr.join('-')) — burn in the Python order: sep.join(list).
split on an explicit delimiter keeps empty pieces — two commas in a row produce an empty string between them. (Only the no-argument split(), which splits on whitespace runs, drops empties.)
split() with NO argument splits on any run of whitespace and discards leading/trailing/empty pieces — the go-to for tokenizing messy text. (split(' ') with an explicit space would keep the empties.)
Strings are immutable: replace() returns a NEW string and leaves s untouched. Because the result isn't assigned, it's thrown away and s is still 'hello'. To keep it: s = s.replace('l', 'L').
s[:3] means 'from the start up to (but not including) index 3' — characters 0, 1, 2 = 'int'. The stop index is always excluded.
A negative start counts from the end: -4 is the 4th char from the right, and with no stop the slice runs to the end — 'view'. Slicing never raises for out-of-range bounds and returns a new string.
[::-1] is the idiomatic full reverse: no start/stop, step -1 walks the sequence backwards, producing a new reversed string (or list). This is the one slicing trick interviewers expect on sight.
The same slice syntax works on lists and returns a NEW list. [1:4] gives indices 1, 2, 3 — the stop (4) is excluded. Getting that exclusive stop wrong is the classic off-by-one.
With a negative step the slice walks backwards from start (4) toward stop (1), and stop is STILL excluded — so you get 4, 3, 2, not 1. Negative-step stops trip almost everyone.
key=len sorts by each element's length rather than its value: 'a'(1), 'bb'(2), 'ccc'(3). The key function is called once per element and Python sorts by what it returns.

The tuple key sorts by count DESCENDING (that's the -p[1]) then name ASCENDING (p[0]): the two 2s come first, ordered a then c, and the 1 last. This 'count desc, then name asc' line is the single most-asked sorting pattern.
list.sort() sorts IN PLACE and returns None — so x is None, not the sorted list. Assigning the result of .sort() is a classic bug; use sorted(...) when you want the sorted list back as a value.

sorted() returns a NEW sorted list and leaves the original untouched — so the sorted view prints first, then nums is still [3, 1, 2]. That non-mutation is exactly why sorted() is the safer default over .sort().
Every element has length 2, so all keys tie — and Python's sort is STABLE, meaning tied elements keep their original order: bb, aa, cc unchanged. Stability is what makes multi-key sorting reliable.

max (and min) take the same key= as sorted: here it compares each pair by its second element and returns the whole pair with the largest one — ('b', 3). You get the element back, not just the key's value.

questions.code:
from itertools import accumulate
print(list(accumulate([2, 1, 3], max)))
questions.explain: accumulate with the max function yields a RUNNING max: max so far after each element — 2, then max(2,1)=2, then max(2,3)=3. With no function it gives a running sum. A tidy itertools tool for cumulative results.

questions.prompt: render(['a', 'b']) crashes with AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'join'. What is the bug?
choices: join is a STRING method, not a list method — call it on the separator: '-'.join(parts)
parts must be a tuple, not a list
you must write parts.join() with no argument
questions.explain: In Python, join belongs to the separator string: '-'.join(parts). A list has no .join(). This backwards-from-JS spelling (arr.join('-')) is the #1 string tell that someone doesn't write much Python — make sep.join(list) automatic.

questions.prompt: This works, but a reviewer flags it for large inputs. What is the accepted criticism?
choices: strings are immutable, so each += may copy everything built so far — O(n^2) worst case; collect the pieces in a list and ''.join(words)
+= on a string mutates the caller's list as a side effect
you must use out.append(w) inside the loop
strings cannot be concatenated inside a loop at all
questions.explain: A str can't be modified, so conceptually every += allocates a new string and copies both halves — quadratic over n pieces. ''.join(words) is guaranteed linear and is what a reviewer expects. (CPython sometimes optimises += in place, but that's an implementation detail that vanishes the moment a second reference exists.)

questions.prompt: smallest([3, 1, 2]) crashes with "'NoneType' object is not subscriptable". Why?
choices: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, so [0] tries to index None; use sorted(xs)[0], or xs.sort() then return xs[0]
xs must be guaranteed non-empty first
sort() needs a key argument to work
[0] should be [-1] to get the smallest
questions.explain: xs.sort() returns None (it mutates in place), and None[0] is the crash. Either use the expression form sorted(xs)[0], or sort in place on its own line and then index xs[0]. This is the return-None trap from L1, now biting a slice.

questions.prompt: last_two([1, 2, 3, 4]) should return the last two items but returns only [3]. What is the bug?
choices: a slice's stop is EXCLUSIVE, and -1 stops just before the final element; drop the stop — xs[-2:] runs to the end
negative indices are not allowed as slice bounds
xs[-2:-1] makes a copy that drops an element
questions.explain: xs[-2:-1] starts at the second-to-last and stops BEFORE the last (stop is exclusive), yielding a single element. To include the end, omit the stop: xs[-2:]. Exclusive-stop off-by-ones are the most common slicing mistake.

questions.prompt: count_letters('banana') is supposed to count each letter but returns wrong counts like {'b': 1, 'a': 1, 'n': 1}. What is the flaw?
choices: groupby only groups CONSECUTIVE equal keys, so 'banana' splits into many one-letter runs and the dict keeps only the last count per letter; sort first (groupby(sorted(s))) or just use collections.Counter(s)
groupby returns its keys in random order
len(list(g)) consumes the group so the next one is empty
dict comprehensions cannot iterate over groupby
questions.explain: groupby groups only ADJACENT equal keys. 'banana' is b-a-n-a-n-a, so every letter is its own run; the dict comprehension then overwrites each key, keeping the last (count 1). Either sort s first so equal letters are adjacent, or reach for collections.Counter(s), which is clearer for plain counting.

questions.prompt: True or false: strings in Python are immutable, so every string method returns a new string and never modifies the original.
questions.explain: True — s.lower(), s.replace(...), s.strip() all return NEW strings; s is unchanged unless you reassign it. The practical fallout: build big strings with ''.join, not += in a loop, because each concatenation makes a fresh copy.

questions.prompt: True or false: sorted() returns a new list and works on any iterable, while list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
questions.explain: True — sorted(iterable, key=...) gives you a new list from any iterable (tuples, sets, dict keys, generators); list.sort() only works on a list, mutates it, and returns None. Prefer sorted() when you want a value back or must not touch the original.

questions.prompt: True or false: in a slice s[a:b], the element at index b is included in the result.
questions.explain: False — the stop index is EXCLUSIVE: s[a:b] includes a but stops just before b. So s[1:4] gives indices 1, 2, 3. This exclusive stop (also true with negative steps) is the classic off-by-one.

questions.prompt: True or false: Python's sort is stable — elements whose sort keys are equal keep their original relative order.
questions.explain: True — Timsort (used by both sorted and list.sort) is stable. That's what makes 'sort by the secondary key first, then the primary' work, and why a tuple key like (-count, name) reliably breaks ties the way you intend.

questions.prompt: True or false: the correct way to join a list of strings is separator.join(list) — a plain list has no .join() method.
questions.explain: True — join lives on the separator string: '-'.join(parts). Lists have no .join(). Writing parts.join('-') (the JS habit) raises AttributeError; make sep.join(list) a reflex.
